pairs.source_text: Ad ea Antonius Primus (is acerrimus belli concitator) festinationem ipsis utilem, Vitellio exitiosam disseruit.
pairs.question: Quis dux partium Flavianarum, quem Tacitus acerrimum belli concitatorem appellat, festinationem belli adversus Vitellium suasit?
pairs.question_en: Which leader of the Flavian party, whom Tacitus calls the keenest instigator of the war, argued for haste in the war against Vitellius?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to the Flavian party + the man who pressed for speed; single named person, supported verbatim by 'Antonius Primus (is acerrimus belli concitator) festinationem ipsis utilem, Vitellio exitiosam disseruit'. Closed-book: Antonius Primus, the Flavian general who drove the Danubian legions into Italy in AD 69, is a stock figure of the year of the four emperors. The Tacitean tag 'acerrimus belli concitator' is reused as the anchor.

pairs.source_text: Quaesitum inde quae sedes bello legeretur. Verona potior visa, patentibus circum campis ad pugnam equestrem, qua praevalebant: simul coloniam copiis validam auferre Vitellio in rem famamque videbatur.
pairs.question: Quam urbem duces Flaviani sedem bello legerunt, propter campos circum patentis equestri pugnae aptos, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Which city did the Flavian leaders choose as the seat of the war, on account of the open plains around it suited to cavalry battle, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to the Flavian leaders + their choice of base; single named place, supported verbatim by 'Verona potior visa, patentibus circum campis ad pugnam equestrem'. Mirrors the source's 'sedes bello legeretur'. Closed-book: Verona as the Flavian rallying-point before the advance on Cremona is a fixed point of the AD 69 campaign.

pairs.source_text: per quadriduum Cremona suffecit. cum omnia sacra profanaque in igne considerent, solum Mefitis templum stetit ante moenia, loco seu numine defensum.
pairs.question: Quod unum templum, ceteris omnibus Cremonae igne consumptis, ante moenia incolume stetit, ut Tacitus refert?
pairs.question_en: Which single temple, when all the rest of Cremona was consumed by fire, stood unharmed before the walls, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Cremona's burning + the one surviving temple; single named cult site, supported verbatim by 'solum Mefitis templum stetit ante moenia'. Closed-book: that only the temple of Mefitis survived the sack of Cremona is a memorable Tacitean detail. 'quod templum... stetit' indicative direct question.

pairs.source_text: per quadriduum Cremona suffecit. cum omnia sacra profanaque in igne considerent, solum Mefitis templum stetit ante moenia, loco seu numine defensum.
pairs.question: Per quot dies, capta urbe, direptio atque incendium Cremonae duravit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: For how many days did the sack of Cremona last, after the city was taken, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Cremona + the duration of its sack; single number, supported verbatim by 'per quadriduum Cremona suffecit' (Cremona held out / sufficed for the plundering four days). 'per quot dies' mirrors the durative 'per quadriduum'. Closed-book: the four-day sack and burning of Cremona by the victorious Flavian army is a notorious atrocity of AD 69.

pairs.source_text: Hic exitus Cremonae anno ducentesimo octogesimo sexto a primordio sui.
pairs.question: Quoto anno a primordio suo urbs Cremona, a Flavianis direpta atque incensa, deleta est, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: In which year from its founding was the city of Cremona, sacked and burned by the Flavians, destroyed, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Cremona + its destruction; single ordinal number, supported verbatim by 'Hic exitus Cremonae anno ducentesimo octogesimo sexto a primordio sui'. Closed-book: Tacitus's dating of Cremona's fall to its 286th year is a stock fact marking the colony's age. 'quoto anno' mirrors the ordinal idiom.

pairs.source_text: sedem Iovis Optimi Maximi auspicato a maioribus pignus imperii conditam, quam non Porsenna dedita urbe neque Galli capta temerare potuissent, furore principum excindi.
pairs.question: Cuius dei aedes in Capitolio, dum Vitelliani et Flaviani Romae armis contendunt, incensa est, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: The temple of which god on the Capitol was burned while the Vitellians and Flavians fought in arms at Rome, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to the Capitol + the deity whose temple burned; single named god, supported verbatim by 'sedem Iovis Optimi Maximi... furore principum excindi' (confirmed at 3.71 'sic Capitolium... conflagravit' and 3.72 'ea tunc aedes cremabatur'). Closed-book: the burning of the temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus during the Flavian assault on Rome in AD 69 is one of the most famous calamities of the civil wars.

pairs.source_text: voverat Tarquinius Priscus rex bello Sabino, ieceratque fundamenta spe magis futurae magnitudinis quam quo modicae adhuc populi Romani res sufficerent.
pairs.question: Quis rex Romanus aedem Iovis Optimi Maximi bello Sabino vovit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Which Roman king vowed the temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus during the Sabine war, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to the temple of Jupiter O.M. + the king who vowed it; single named person, supported verbatim by 'voverat Tarquinius Priscus rex bello Sabino, ieceratque fundamenta' (antecedent: 'sedem Iovis Optimi Maximi' earlier in 3.72). Closed-book: that Tarquinius Priscus vowed and laid the foundations of the Capitoline temple of Jupiter is a stock fact of Roman tradition. 'vovit' + accusative.

pairs.source_text: At primores civitatis Flavium Sabinum praefectum urbis secretis sermonibus incitabant, victoriae famaeque partem capesseret.
pairs.question: Quod munus Romae Flavius Sabinus, Vespasiani frater, eo tempore gerebat, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Which office at Rome did Flavius Sabinus, Vespasian's brother, hold at that time, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Flavius Sabinus + brother of Vespasian + his office; single named magistracy, supported verbatim by 'Flavium Sabinum praefectum urbis'. Closed-book: Flavius Sabinus, the elder brother of Vespasian and prefect of the city, killed in the Flavian struggle for Rome in AD 69, is a fixed figure of the year. 'praefecturam urbis' answers 'quod munus gerebat'.

pairs.source_text: innocentiam iustitiamque eius non argueres; sermonis nimius erat: id unum septem annis quibus Moesiam, duodecim quibus praefecturam urbis obtinuit, calumniatus est rumor.
pairs.question: Per quot annos Flavius Sabinus praefecturam urbis obtinuit, ut Tacitus refert?
pairs.question_en: For how many years did Flavius Sabinus hold the prefecture of the city, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Flavius Sabinus + the duration of his city prefecture; single number, supported verbatim by 'duodecim quibus praefecturam urbis obtinuit' (subject Sabinus, 'Hic exitus viri', 3.75). Closed-book number fact about Vespasian's brother's long tenure as praefectus urbi.

pairs.source_text: Domitianus prima inruptione apud aedituum occultatus, sollertia liberti lineo amictu turbae sacricolarum immixtus ignoratusque, apud Cornelium Primum paternum clientem iuxta Velabrum delituit.
pairs.question: Quis filius Vespasiani, capta a Vitellianis Capitolii arce, lineo amictu inter sacricolas occultatus evasit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Which son of Vespasian escaped, hidden in a linen garment among the temple-worshippers, when the citadel of the Capitol was taken by the Vitellians, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to the son of Vespasian + his escape from the Capitol; single named person, supported verbatim by 'Domitianus... lineo amictu turbae sacricolarum immixtus ignoratusque... delituit'. Closed-book: Domitian's escape in disguise from the burning Capitol, before becoming emperor, is a famous episode of AD 69.

pairs.source_text: fessusque misero errore et pudenda latebra semet occultans ab Iulio Placido tribuno cohortis protrahitur.
pairs.question: Quis tribunus cohortis Vitellium in Palatio latentem protraxit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Which cohort tribune dragged Vitellius out as he hid in the Palace, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Vitellius + the man who hauled him from hiding; single named person, supported verbatim by 'ab Iulio Placido tribuno cohortis protrahitur' (subject Vitellius, from 'in Palatium regreditur' earlier in 3.84). Closed-book: Vitellius's discovery in a wretched hiding place at the fall of Rome is a stock scene of his end.

pairs.source_text: postremo ad Gemonias, ubi corpus Flavii Sabini iacuerat, propulere. una vox non degeneris animi excepta, cum tribuno insultanti se tamen imperatorem eius fuisse respondit; ac deinde ingestis vulneribus concidit.
pairs.question: Quo loco Vitellium milites propulerunt, ubi antea Flavii Sabini corpus iacuerat, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: To what place did the soldiers drive Vitellius, where the body of Flavius Sabinus had earlier lain, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Vitellius + the place of his death + the prior fate of Sabinus's body; single named place, supported verbatim by 'postremo ad Gemonias, ubi corpus Flavii Sabini iacuerat, propulere'. Closed-book: Vitellius killed and his body cast on the Gemoniae, where Sabinus's body had lain, is the famous end of his reign.

pairs.source_text: septimum et quinquagensimum aetatis annum explebat, consulatum, sacerdotia, nomen locumque inter primores nulla sua industria, sed cuncta patris claritudine adeptus.
pairs.question: Quotum aetatis annum Vitellius, cum periit, explebat, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Which year of his life was Vitellius completing when he died, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Vitellius + his age at death; single ordinal number, supported verbatim by 'septimum et quinquagensimum aetatis annum explebat' (subject Vitellius, just killed in 3.85). 'quotum aetatis annum... explebat' mirrors the source idiom. Closed-book biographical number, parallel to the recorded ages of the other emperors of AD 69.

pairs.source_text: Isdem diebus Fabius Valens Vrbini in custodia interficitur. caput eius Vitellianis cohortibus ostentatum ne quam ultra spem foverent.
pairs.question: In qua urbe Fabius Valens, dux Vitellianus, in custodia interfectus est, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: In which town was Fabius Valens, the Vitellian general, killed while in custody, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Fabius Valens + the Vitellian command + the place of his death; single named place, supported verbatim by 'Fabius Valens Vrbini in custodia interficitur' (Vrbini = locative of Urbinum). Closed-book: the capture and execution of the Vitellian general Fabius Valens at Urbinum, his severed head shown to his troops, is a key turning point before Rome's fall.

pairs.source_text: Cartimandua Brigantibus imperitabat, pollens nobilitate; et auxerat potentiam, postquam capto per dolum rege Carataco instruxisse triumphum Claudii Caesaris videbatur.
pairs.question: Cui genti Britanniae Cartimandua regina imperabat, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Which people of Britain did Queen Cartimandua rule, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Queen Cartimandua + the people she ruled; single named people, supported verbatim by 'Cartimandua Brigantibus imperitabat, pollens nobilitate'. 'imperabat' + dative mirrors 'imperitabat'. Closed-book: Cartimandua, queen of the Brigantes who handed over Caratacus, is a stock figure of Roman Britain.
